name: libcpr/cpr
description: Evaluation questions for cpr, a C++ Requests library (spiritual port of Python Requests, wrapping libcurl). Held-out C++ corpus written from reading the real source in eval_repos/cpr, independent of RepoGuide's C++ semantic provider implementation -- not tuned against provider output.

questions.question: What are cpr's core types and how do they relate to each other?
questions.expectedAnswer: `Session` holds one HTTP session's configuration and connection state; calling one of its methods (`Get()`, `Post()`, etc.) executes a request and returns a `Response`. The package-level template free functions `cpr::Get(...)`/`cpr::Post(...)` are convenience wrappers: each constructs a fresh `Session`, applies the caller's variadic options to it via `priv::set_option`, then calls the matching `Session` method and returns its `Response`.

questions.question: cpr's `Body`/`Url`/`Interface` classes all inherit from `StringHolder<T>` with `T` being the derived class itself, and `StringHolder`'s own constructors are private. What C++ idiom is this, and how does it still let `Body` construct itself?
questions.expectedAnswer: This is the CRTP (Curiously Recurring Template Pattern): `class Body : public StringHolder<Body>`. `StringHolder`'s constructors are private, but it declares `friend T;` for its own template parameter -- meaning only the exact derived class instantiating it (here, `Body`) is granted friendship and can call those private constructors from its own constructor's initializer list. This is a compile-time-enforced way of saying "only my own derived class may construct me," with zero virtual-dispatch cost.

questions.question: How is cpr's source organized -- are class declarations and their implementations in the same file?
questions.expectedAnswer: No -- cpr follows the classic C++ header/source split: class declarations (with method prototypes, no bodies) live under `include/cpr/*.h`, and their out-of-class `ClassName::method(...)` implementations live in a separate, same-basename `.cpp` file directly under `cpr/` (e.g. `include/cpr/cookies.h` + `cpr/cookies.cpp`). This is the dominant convention in this codebase, not an occasional pattern.

questions.question: Where is the Cookie class declared?
Where is the Session class declared?
Where is Session::Get()'s real implementation (not just its declaration)?
questions.expectedAnswer: In `cpr/session.cpp`, line 782 -- `Session::Get()` is only declared (prototyped) in `include/cpr/session.h`; its actual body is defined out-of-class in the paired `.cpp` file.

questions.question: Where is the DerCert class declared, and what does it inherit from?
Where is the top-level cpr::Get() template free function declared?
Trace what happens when you call the package-level cpr::Get(...) function.
questions.expectedAnswer: `Get(Ts&&... ts)` (in `include/cpr/api.h`) constructs a fresh, default `Session`, applies every caller-supplied option to it via `priv::set_option(session, ...)` (a variadic-template helper that dispatches each option to the right `Session::SetOption`/`UpdateHeader` overload), then calls `session.Get()` and returns its `Response`. A brand-new `Session` is created on every call, mirroring reqwest's/resty's own "convenience function creates a fresh client" pattern.

expectedFlow.description: Template free function constructing a fresh Session, applying options, then delegating to Session::Get().

questions.question: What does Session::Get() actually do, step by step?
questions.expectedAnswer: Its entire body (defined in `cpr/session.cpp`, not the header) is two calls: `PrepareGet()` (sets up the request for a GET, e.g. clearing any body/method-specific curl options left over from a prior call on the same session) followed by `return makeRequest();`, which performs the actual libcurl request and builds the `Response`. `Session::Post()`/`Head()`/`Options()`/`Patch()` all follow the identical two-step shape with their own `Prepare*()` call.

expectedFlow.description: A thin per-verb method preparing method-specific curl state, then delegating to one shared request-execution method.

questions.question: How does Body's constructor from a std::string actually initialize the object, given Body inherits from StringHolder<Body>?
questions.expectedAnswer: `Body(std::string body) : StringHolder<Body>(std::move(body)) {}` -- the constructor body is empty; all real initialization is delegated to the private `StringHolder<Body>` base-class constructor via the member-initializer list, which `Body` is allowed to call only because `StringHolder` grants `friend T` (i.e. `friend Body`) to its own template parameter.

expectedFlow.description: A derived CRTP class's constructor delegating entirely to its private base-class constructor, permitted via a template-parameter friend declaration.

questions.question: Cookie::GetExpiresString needs to format a time_point as a string on both Windows and non-Windows platforms -- how does it branch?
questions.expectedAnswer: It converts the stored `expires_` time_point to a `std::time_t`, then uses a preprocessor conditional (`#ifdef _WIN32` / `#else`) to call the platform-appropriate thread-safe conversion function: `gmtime_s(&tm, &tt)` on Windows (which has a different argument order/return convention than POSIX), or `gmtime_r(&tt, &tm)` everywhere else, before formatting the resulting `std::tm` with a `std::stringstream`.

expectedFlow.description: Preprocessor-conditional platform branch selecting between Windows's and POSIX's differently-shaped thread-safe gmtime functions.

questions.question: Explain cpr::Get(...), step by step.
questions.expectedAnswer: It's a variadic template function taking any number of forwarding-reference arguments. It default-constructs a local `Session`, forwards every argument into `priv::set_option(session, ...)` (which recursively dispatches each argument to the matching `Session::SetOption` overload or, for a second `Header` argument, `UpdateHeader` instead, to merge rather than overwrite), and finally calls `session.Get()` and returns its `Response` directly -- no explicit error handling of its own; errors surface through the returned `Response`'s own error field.

questions.question: Why does StringHolder declare `friend T;` five times, once per constructor, instead of once for the class?
questions.expectedAnswer: Each `friend T;` line sits directly above one specific private constructor overload (default, from `std::string`, from `std::string_view`, from `const char*`, and from a `const char*` + length pair) -- but in C++, `friend` grants access to ALL private members of the class, not just the constructor it's textually adjacent to, so the repetition is stylistic/documentation-adjacent (signaling "this constructor exists for the derived type to use") rather than five functionally distinct grants. All five ultimately have the same effect: only the class's own template parameter `T` (the concrete derived type, e.g. `Body`) can construct a `StringHolder<T>`.

questions.question: What is cpr_pf_arg_t, and why is it defined with a preprocessor conditional instead of a single typedef?
questions.expectedAnswer: `cpr_pf_arg_t` is the argument type libcurl's progress-callback expects. Its doc comment says it's "dependent on libcurl version": on libcurl versions older than 7.32.0 (`LIBCURL_VERSION_NUM < 0x072000`) it's `double`, matching the legacy progress-callback signature; on newer versions it's `cpr_off_t` (a wrapper around curl's own `curl_off_t`), matching the modern signature. The conditional exists because this is a real ABI/API difference in libcurl itself across versions, not something cpr can paper over with one definition.

questions.question: Where does cpr implement a GraphQL query builder?
questions.expectedAnswer: It doesn't -- cpr is a general-purpose HTTP/REST client wrapping libcurl; there is no GraphQL-specific query construction or execution anywhere in its source (confirmed: no case-insensitive match for "graphql" anywhere under include/ or cpr/).

questions.question: Does cpr support WebSocket connections?
questions.expectedAnswer: No -- cpr is built around libcurl's HTTP request/response model; there is no WebSocket handshake, frame handling, or persistent-connection support anywhere in the source (confirmed: no match for "websocket" anywhere in the codebase).

questions.question: Does cpr implement its own TLS/SSL handshake or cryptographic primitives?
questions.expectedAnswer: No -- TLS is entirely delegated to libcurl's own TLS backend (configured via cpr's `SslOptions`/`ssl_options.h`, which just wraps curl's own SSL-related `CURLOPT_*` settings like certificate/key file paths). cpr implements no cryptography or handshake logic of its own.

questions.question: I just edited cpr/session.cpp locally but haven't reindexed. Which Session methods does it define, and could the index be stale for them?
questions.expectedAnswer: It defines the out-of-class implementations of `Session::Get`, `Session::Head`, `Session::Options`, `Session::Patch`, `Session::Post`, and others -- their declarations live in `include/cpr/session.h`, but their real bodies are here. Since this file was just modified without reindexing, any cached understanding of these methods' bodies -- including this answer -- may be stale and should be re-verified against the current file contents.
